displayQuote: Americans are so enamored of equality that they would rather be equal in slavery than unequal in freedom

meta.title: Who really said "Americans are so enamored of equality that they would rather be equal in slavery than unequal in freedom"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: A rewrite, not a quotation. Tocqueville wrote that a depraved taste for equality “reduces men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom” — of the human heart, not of Americans.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Americans are so enamored of equality that they would rather be equal in slavery than unequal in freedom'?
meta.ogDescription: Tocqueville really wrote this — almost. The 1835 sentence is about “the human heart,” not about Americans, and the popular wording is a modern compression.

answer.label: Not his wording — and he wasn’t talking about Americans
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Tocqueville’s and it is easy to find: Democracy in America, Volume I (1835), Chapter III. But he wrote it of the human heart, not of Americans — “there exists also in the human heart a depraved taste for equality … and reduces men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom.” The familiar one-liner compresses that sentence and swaps in a nation as its subject.

source.heading: The sentence he actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Henry Reeve, 1835 — the standard English text
Chapter III, “Social Condition of the Anglo-Americans” — section “Political Consequences of the Social Condition of the Anglo-Americans”

source.excerpt: There is, in fact, a manly and lawful passion for equality which excites men to wish all to be powerful and honored. This passion tends to elevate the humble to the rank of the great; but there exists also in the human heart a depraved taste for equality, which impels the weak to attempt to lower the powerful to their own level, and reduces men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom.
trail: Project Gutenberg’s full text of Volume I — Henry Reeve’s translation, from the London: Saunders and Otley edition of 1835 — carries the passage in Chapter III: a depraved taste for equality “reduces men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom.”

In that same paragraph the subject is “the human heart,” and the sentence immediately after it says of democratic nations that “on the contrary, they have an instinctive love” of liberty — so reading the line as a verdict on Americans inverts the surrounding argument (Chapter III, Project Gutenberg).

Wikiquote’s Tocqueville page prints the genuine passage and appends the popular sentence beneath it under the note “Often misquoted as” — an independent record that the circulating wording is a misquotation rather than a translation variant.

A site search of Quote Investigator for this wording returns nothing — the specialists have not investigated this line, and the earliest wording we were able to confirm ourselves is Reeve’s 1835 translation above.
source.cutTag: ↑ Reeve’s 1835 translation, Volume I, Chapter III
source.excerptNote: The popular version squeezes this into one line and changes its subject. Tocqueville locates the impulse in “the human heart”; the quotation card locates it in Americans.

author.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
author.heading: About Alexis de Tocqueville
author.metaLine: 1805–1859 · French magistrate, political thinker and author of Democracy in America
author.bio: Alexis de Tocqueville sailed for the United States in 1831 as a young French magistrate nominally studying American prisons, and came home with something far larger: De la démocratie en Amérique, published in two volumes in 1835 and 1840. Its subject is not really America but equality — what a society gains and what it risks when rank dissolves. Henry Reeve’s English translation appeared alongside the French, and it is Reeve’s wording that most English quotations of Tocqueville ultimately descend from, however far they have since drifted.

copyAttribution: "Americans are so enamored of equality that they would rather be equal in slavery than unequal in freedom" is a modern paraphrase, not Tocqueville’s wording. In Democracy in America, vol. 1 (trans. Henry Reeve; London: Saunders and Otley, 1835), ch. III, he wrote that a “depraved taste for equality … reduces men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom” — a claim about the human heart, not about Americans.

misattribution.heading: What the popular version changes
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — the thought really is Tocqueville’s. What travels is a rewrite that tightens his sentence and, in tightening it, changes what it is about.

items.why: The compressed, quotable form found on quotation cards and in speeches. It is not Reeve’s wording, nor any translation wording we could locate; Wikiquote lists it explicitly as a misquotation of the passage below.

items.who: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, Vol. I (1835)
items.why: “… there exists also in the human heart a depraved taste for equality, which impels the weak to attempt to lower the powerful to their own level, and reduces men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom.” (Chapter III, Project Gutenberg)

Tocqueville is describing a temptation he thinks universal, in a chapter about what equality does to any society. The popular version turns a claim about human nature into a charge against one nation — which is why it reads as an insult, and why it is so often quoted as one (Chapter III, Project Gutenberg).

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: Tocqueville did write that men can be reduced “to prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom” — Democracy in America, Vol. I, Chapter III — but he said it of the human heart, not of Americans, and not in these words.

context.heading: Why the rewrite sticks
lead: Tocqueville came to the United States in 1831 to study its prisons and left convinced that the real story was equality — not as a slogan but as a solvent, dissolving rank and, with it, some of the ballast that had held liberty in place. Chapter III of Volume I is where he first states the danger plainly, and it is deliberately general: the appetite for levelling belongs to “the human heart,” everywhere.

The rewritten line is more useful than the original to anyone arguing about America, which is precisely why it spread. It converts a diagnosis of human nature into a verdict on a country, and it lends a nineteenth-century Frenchman’s authority to a modern complaint he did not make.
context.pull: He wrote it about the human heart. The internet re-addressed the envelope.
